message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I did the right thing or not in this situation. Let me start by understanding what happened. A few years ago, I was renting a place with this dude, and we were on a lease. When the lease was ending, he just left without giving much notice. He took most of his stuff, leaving only the last bit of his half of the rent and a few things he mentioned in a note that he didn't want to bring with him. Now, where I live, if you don't get rid of your stuff when you move out, the landlord can pay someone to remove it, and that cost comes out of your deposit. I've heard of cases where people have $250 taken off their deposit just for someone to take three milk crates of stuff to the dump. That's a rip-off. So, I texted and emailed him for two weeks asking him to pick up his stuff, and if he didn't, I was going to take them to the dump. But he never responded. So, I took most of his stuff to the dump, but he also had around 60 video games for the PS4. I figured I'd sell them. There's a local game store that buys used games, and they gave me $600 for all of his games. Fast forward to last week, I was at a party he was at, and we were being polite. Then he asked how the move-out was, and I said it was good. Naturally, he asked what I did with his stuff. He got mad when he found out I sold his games, but I told him that I tried to get him to grab those things, but he never reached out. Now he's calling me an asshole and asking me to pay him back. I checked, and legally, there's nothing wrong with what I did, but now I'm wondering if I'm the asshole for doing this. Alright, so to break this down, I need to consider a few things: 1. **Communication**: Did I make reasonable efforts to contact him about his stuff? 2. **Legal Rights**: Was selling his games within my legal rights as a roommate? 3. **Ethical Considerations**: Even if it's legal, was it the right thing to do? 4. **Consequences**: How has this affected our relationship, and what can I do now? Starting with communication, I texted and emailed him for two weeks. That seems like a reasonable effort. I gave him ample time to respond. If he didn't, it's not my fault, right? But maybe I should have tried calling him or left a note somewhere else. Legally, I think in most places, if someone leaves their stuff behind, you can dispose of it, especially if it's causing a problem for the landlord. But selling it for money might be a gray area. I'm not sure if I had the right to sell his games without his permission, even if I was trying to avoid the landlord charging me. Ethically, even if it's legal, selling someone's stuff without their consent feels a bit underhanded. I mean, he left the games behind, but that doesn't necessarily mean he wanted to get rid of them. Maybe he just didn't want to take them with him at the time. Selling them for $600 is a lot of money, and now he's upset because he feels like he lost something valuable. As for the consequences, our relationship is definitely strained now. He's calling me names and asking for money back. I don't want to be enemies, but I also don't want to be seen as the bad guy here. Maybe I should have handled it differently. Perhaps instead of selling the games, I could have stored them somewhere and waited longer for him to claim them. Or, if I was really worried about the landlord charging me, I could have talked to him about it and see if we could split the cost or find another solution. In the end, I think I did what I thought was best at the time, but maybe there was a better way to handle it that would have kept our relationship intact. I should consider how my actions affected him and whether there's a way to make things right, even if it's just apologizing for the way things went down. I also need to think about the future. If I ever find myself in a similar situation, how can I handle it in a way that's fair to both parties and maintains respect? Maybe setting clearer expectations upfront or having a conversation about what to do with belongings if someone moves out unexpectedly. Overall, while I might not be legally in the wrong, ethically and relationally, I could have handled it better. It's a lesson in communication and considering others' feelings, even when you're trying to do the right thing.
